flags.evidence: Opened page/index.html from disk with Playwright at 1440x900 and 390x844 (DSF 3). The most prominent first-screen action is the filled button 'Send me alerts for my street' (1440: y=724; 390: y=755), repeated by the header button 'Get alerts for your street' (href #signup, which only scrolls to the form). Chose 'Oakdale', typed ana@example.com, clicked the button: no page error, and script.js navigated to 'mailto:alerts@commonread.org?subject=Alerts%20for%20Oakdale&body=Please%20add%20me...'. The #signup-done panel then showed 'Almost there. Your email app should have opened... If nothing opened, email alerts@commonread.org'. The brief supplies no email address or domain, so the primary action goes to an email address the brief did not supply, which the table counts. The exception for a local action whose result is stated up front does not apply: the only text next to the button before the click is 'Free. At most one email per meeting. Reply "stop" to stop.', which never says the button opens an email app, and in any case this is not a local action. Same result at both widths.

Read the page at 1440 and 390 and searched its text for 'sample', 'example', 'illustrative', 'fictional' and 'demo'. The only hit is an unrelated mention of 'a sample of corrected summaries'. In the #how section the intro says 'Here is one real item from the October 28 agenda, next to the summary we sent', and the summary beside it reads 'Checked against the original by Dana R. (volunteer), Oct 24'. In the #clerks section ('For city clerks and funders: where we are') the pilot table states 'City: Linden Falls (one city so far)' and 'Meetings covered: Every regular council meeting since September 2026'. The brief names no city and says there are no usage numbers to show. This is an invented track record and invented operating history, shown as fact to clerks and funders, which counts as a usage claim not supplied by the brief. The linked agenda/2026-10-28-item-7b.html calls itself 'A copy of the city's posted agenda, kept by Commonread for the pilot'. Because the content calls itself real, it is the opposite of the 'clearly labelled sample data' exception. The brief supports none of it, so the 'plain statements of status' exception does not apply either. The only labelled example is the hero alert card ('What an alert looks like'), and it does not cover these sections.
